extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners/readers of MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Alice/Mayo-style subject matter eligibility analysis and drafting complete written 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections (Steps 2A Prong One, 2A Prong Two, and 2B), including evidentiary support and form paragraph usage. Targets how examiners should identify exceptions, evaluate additional elements, and document findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) the judicial exception. The rejection must explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception (e.g., a law of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information about Step 2A. Provide a reasoned rationale identifying what subject matter the limitations describe when the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception. Sample explanation: 'The claim recites the step of comparing collected information to a predefined threshold, which is an act of evaluating information that can be practically performed in the human mind. Thus, this step is an abstract idea in the “mental process” grouping.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify abstract ideas as recited and tie to abstract-idea groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited in the claim and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2), or follow the tentative abstract idea procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the abstract idea as recited in claim language and explain why it falls within a grouping. If the limitation does not fall within the enumerated groupings, use the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure (MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)). While not required, the explanation may cite an appropriate court decision that supports the identification, but examiners should be familiar with any cited decision and avoid relying upon language taken out of context or non-precedential decisions unless facts match uniquely. See USPTO court-decision chart at www.uspto.gov/PatentEligibility. Sample language: identify the recited limitation and explain why it is a mental process, mathematical concept, or method of organizing human activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify laws of nature or natural phenomena as recited and explain rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify that law or phenomenon as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain using a reasoned rationale why the recited subject matter is a law of nature or natural phenomenon. See MPEP § 2106.04(b). Sample: 'The claim recites the correlation of X, and X is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body.' When the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the exception, explain what subject matter is described and why it is an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify products of nature and perform markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to how the product of nature is recited in the claim and compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine if there are markedly different characteristics (MPEP § 2106.04(b),(c)). Sample: 'X was isolated from naturally occurring Y. Because there is no indication in the record that isolation resulted in a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties as compared to its counterpart, X is a product of nature exception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional claim elements do not integrate the exception or add significantly more (Step 2A Prong Two & Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the exception and explain why they do not integrate the exception into a practical application and do not add significantly more to the exception. The explanation should address additional elements both individually and in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. Remember that a new combination of known steps may be eligible (Diamond v. Diehr). Address whether additional elements meaningfully limit the exception. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 for considerations. Provide reasoned rationale so applicant can respond; when appropriate, explain why additional elements do integrate the exception or provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. If concluding certain limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional in the relevant field, support that conclusion per Subsection III.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of generic computer components and insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim. Similarly, limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, storing data, or linking to a technological environment) often do not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why generic computing functions (e.g., using the Internet to gather data) or insignificant extra-solution activity do not add a meaningful limitation. Keep in mind case law (e.g., DDR Holdings where generic components in combination performed non-generic functions and were eligible; Parker v. Flook where field-of-use limitation was insufficient). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f),(g),(h) for examples. Provide concrete explanation (e.g., storing data does not meaningfully limit computing a mathematical relationship; placing a product of nature in a test tube is merely a nominal extra-solution component).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary requirements and treatment of eligibility as question of law with possible factual issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts consider eligibility a question of law, and generally do not require 'evidence' to find a claim recites a judicial exception; however, underlying factual issues (e.g., whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional) may arise and when asserting such routine/conventional character the examiner must support that assertion in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Step 2A Prong One, a reasoned rationale is sufficient and no evidence (publications/affidavits) is required to find a claim recites a judicial exception. At Step 2A Prong Two/Step 2B, evidence is not required except when asserting that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, or conventional; in that case, the examiner must support the conclusion in writing using one of the Subsection III options (A)-(D). Cite relevant precedents that describe whether the issue is law or involves factual findings (Rapid Litig. Mgmt.; Berkheimer; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support options when asserting additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (Subsection III: A–D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not assert an additional element is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless they find and expressly support the rejection in writing with one or more of the following: (A) citation to the specification or applicant statement, (B) citation to court decisions, (C) citation to publications, or (D) official notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A: Cite express statements in the specification or applicant prosecution statements showing the element is described as well-understood, routine, or commercially available. Note: silence in the specification is insufficient. B: Cite one or more court decisions that noted the element's routine nature, ensuring the recitation matches the court's terminology and level of generality. C: Cite publications (books, manuals, review articles) that demonstrate the element is widely prevalent or in common use; a single patent/publication is insufficient unless it shows wide prevalence. D: Take official notice only when certain by personal knowledge that the element is widely prevalent/common; follow procedures for official notice (MPEP § 2144.03) and address applicant challenges. See Subsection III for detailed description of each option and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make complete examination under other patentability requirements and state non‑cumulative reasons (compact prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under principles of compact prosecution, regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under each of the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and 101 (utility, inventorship and double patenting) and non-statutory double patenting). Examiners should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure first Office action contains all non-cumulative rejections and bases across applicable statutes to promote compact prosecution. State all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action so applicants can respond effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasoned rationale and avoid reliance on out-of-context or non-precedential authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a rejection, explain the rationale underlying the conclusion so that applicant can effectively respond. Examiners should be familiar with any cited decision relied upon and avoid relying upon language taken out of context or non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the rejection is tied to the facts of the case and avoid using court language out of context. Do not go beyond concepts enumerated as abstract ideas in MPEP § 2106.04 unless using the tentative abstract idea procedure. Avoid reliance on non-precedential decisions unless the facts of the application uniquely match the facts at issue in those decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate form paragraphs and required ordering/content for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified form paragraphs (7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, and 7.05.017 where applicable) when making 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections, and follow the required ordering and content instructions for each form paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.04.01 (Statement of Statutory Basis) must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions/final rejections. Use 7.05 (Rejection, 35 U.S.C. 101 - heading) and follow it with a detailed explanation using 7.05.01, 7.05.016, 7.05.017, etc., as applicable. 7.05.016 is for claims directed to a judicial exception without significantly more and must identify whether claims are directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea and explain the recitation, why it is an exception, why additional elements fail to integrate into a practical application, and why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. If the judicial exception is a tentative abstract idea, include form paragraph 7.05.017 and the TC Director's signature. Follow examiner notes for bracketed content and ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest specification-based claim amendments to overcome eligibility rejections (best practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible, and identify those elements in the Office action and suggest them as a way to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, identify elements from the specification that could be included in claims to provide meaningful limitations or inventive concepts and explicitly suggest such amendments in the Office action to help applicant overcome the rejection.
